choices.text: The point at which the forward and reverse reactions balance each other's progress
The point at which all of the reactants have been used up
choices.why: Most reactions don't go to completion. At equilibrium, reactants and products are both present, and the two reactions balance.

choices.text: The point at which both reactions stop
choices.why: Both reactions keep going at equilibrium; they just cancel each other's progress.

choices.text: The point at which there are equal amounts of reactants and products
choices.why: Equilibrium means the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal, not the amounts.

explanation: Chemical equilibrium is the point at which the forward and reverse processes balance each other's progress, so any continued overall reaction stops.

prompt: H2 and I2 react in a closed container to make HI: H2 + I2 → 2HI. Does all of the H2 and I2 end up as HI?

choices.text: No; the reverse reaction, 2HI → H2 + I2, also takes place and undoes some of the forward reaction.
Yes; the equation shows a single arrow, so the reaction goes to completion.
choices.why: The way the equation is written suggests completion, but the reverse reaction also occurs.

choices.text: No, because the H2 escapes from the container.
choices.why: The container is closed, so nothing escapes. The reverse reaction is what keeps some H2 and I2 present.

choices.text: Yes, but only if the container is heated.
choices.why: The reverse reaction happens regardless; the system reaches equilibrium instead of completion.

explanation: The reverse reaction, 2HI → H2 + I2, also takes place. Eventually it proceeds as fast as the forward reaction, and the system reaches equilibrium with all three substances present.

prompt: As H2 and I2 react to form HI, what happens that eventually brings the system to equilibrium?

choices.text: The reverse reaction speeds up until it matches the speed of the forward reaction.
The forward reaction speeds up until all the reactants are gone.
choices.why: Equilibrium isn't reached by using up the reactants; it's reached when the reverse reaction keeps pace with the forward one.

choices.text: Both reactions slow down until they stop.
choices.why: Neither reaction stops. They run at the same rate.

choices.text: The container fills up, and no more HI can form.
choices.why: Space doesn't limit it. The reverse reaction catches up with the forward reaction.

explanation: The reverse reaction acts to undo what the forward reaction does. Eventually it proceeds as quickly as the forward reaction, and any continued overall reaction stops: equilibrium.

prompt: What does the double arrow in H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI mean?

choices.text: The reaction is going in both directions.
The reaction happens twice.
choices.why: The double arrow shows two opposing processes occurring at once: forward and reverse.

choices.text: The products are twice the reactants.
choices.why: Amounts come from the coefficients, not the arrow.

choices.text: The reaction doesn't need to be balanced.
choices.why: An equilibrium equation must still be balanced.

explanation: Because two opposing processes are occurring at once, an equilibrium is represented with a double arrow, implying the reaction is going in both directions. The equation must still be balanced.

prompt: Why is chemical equilibrium described as dynamic rather than static?

choices.text: Both the forward and reverse reactions keep occurring, at the same rate, so their changes cancel.
The amounts of reactants and products keep changing back and forth.
choices.why: At equilibrium there is no overall change in amounts. The reactions continue, but their effects cancel.

choices.text: The reactions stop completely.
choices.why: That would be a static equilibrium. Chemical equilibrium is dynamic: the reactions keep going.

choices.text: The temperature keeps rising.
choices.why: Dynamic refers to the reactions still taking place, not to temperature.

explanation: At equilibrium, the reactions do not stop; both continue at the same rate, so any overall change by one is canceled by the other. That makes chemical equilibrium dynamic, rather than static.

prompt: A student says that once a reaction reaches equilibrium, the reactant molecules stop reacting. What is wrong?

choices.text: The forward and reverse reactions both continue, at the same rate; only the overall change stops.
Nothing is wrong; equilibrium means the reaction has finished.
choices.why: Equilibrium is dynamic. The reactions still occur; their progress just cancels.

choices.text: At equilibrium only the reverse reaction continues.
choices.why: If only the reverse reaction ran, the amounts would change. Both run, at equal rates.

choices.text: At equilibrium the reactions speed up.
choices.why: The rates don't keep rising; the point is that the forward and reverse rates are equal.

explanation: One thing to note about equilibrium is that the reactions do not stop; both the forward and reverse reactions continue to occur at the same rate.

prompt: A student says that at equilibrium the amounts of reactants and products must be equal. What is wrong?

choices.text: Equilibrium means the forward and reverse rates are equal; the amounts can be quite different.
Nothing is wrong; equal amounts define equilibrium.
choices.why: What's equal at equilibrium is the rates of the two reactions. The amounts just stop changing.

choices.text: At equilibrium there are no reactants left.
choices.why: Reactants and products are both present at equilibrium.

choices.text: At equilibrium there are no products yet.
choices.why: Products form before equilibrium is reached; both are present at equilibrium.

explanation: At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the amounts stop changing. Those amounts need not be equal to each other.

prompt: A reaction in a closed container has reached equilibrium. What do you observe about the amounts of reactants and products over time?

choices.text: They stay constant, even though both reactions continue.
The reactants keep decreasing until they're gone.
choices.why: At equilibrium, any reactant used up by the forward reaction is replaced by the reverse reaction.

choices.text: The products keep increasing.
choices.why: Product formed by the forward reaction is used up at the same rate by the reverse reaction.

choices.text: They swing up and down, back and forth.
choices.why: The two reactions cancel each other's progress continuously, so the amounts stay constant.

explanation: At equilibrium, any overall change by one reaction is canceled by the reverse reaction, so there is no net change in the amounts, though both reactions are still occurring.

prompt: A system is at equilibrium: H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI. Which other way of writing it represents the same equilibrium?

choices.text: 2HI ⇌ H2 + I2
HI ⇌ H2 + I2
choices.why: The equation must still be balanced: 2HI ⇌ H2 + I2.

choices.text: 2HI → H2 + I2
choices.why: A single arrow describes only the reverse reaction. Written backward, it is still an equilibrium: 2HI ⇌ H2 + I2.

choices.text: None; an equilibrium can only be written one way.
choices.why: Because both reactions occur at once, an equilibrium can be written backward.

explanation: Because both reactions are occurring simultaneously, an equilibrium can be written backward: H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI is the same as 2HI ⇌ H2 + I2. The reaction must be at equilibrium for this to be so.

prompt: Which equation represents the equilibrium between PCl5 as the reactant and PCl3 and Cl2 as the products?

choices.text: PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2
PCl5 → PCl3 + Cl2
choices.why: A single arrow suggests the reaction goes to completion. An equilibrium uses a double arrow.

choices.text: PCl5 + ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2
choices.why: The "+" before ⇌ is a stray sign; nothing is added to PCl5.

choices.text: PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + 2Cl2
choices.why: That doesn't balance: there are 5 Cl on the left but 7 on the right.

explanation: An equilibrium is written with a double arrow, and the equation must still be balanced: PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2 has 1 P and 5 Cl on each side.

prompt: Which is a correctly written equilibrium equation between N2O4 as the reactant and NO2 as the product?

choices.text: N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2
N2O4 ⇌ NO2
choices.why: That isn't balanced: 2 N and 4 O on the left, but 1 N and 2 O on the right.

choices.text: N2O4 → 2NO2
choices.why: A single arrow shows only the forward reaction. Equilibrium needs a double arrow.

choices.text: N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 + O2
choices.why: That doesn't balance: there are 4 O on the left and 6 on the right.

explanation: The equilibrium uses a double arrow and must be balanced: N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 has 2 N and 4 O on each side.

prompt: The section considers the reaction of H2 with I2 in a closed container. Why does it matter that the container is closed?

choices.text: No material can go in or out, so the reactants and products stay together and can react in both directions.
A closed container makes the reaction go to completion.
choices.why: Even in a closed container the reaction reaches equilibrium, not completion.

choices.text: A closed container stops the reverse reaction.
choices.why: In a closed container, the products stay present, so the reverse reaction can happen.

choices.text: It doesn't matter; equilibrium is the same in an open container.
choices.why: If a product could escape, it couldn't react in the reverse direction, so the two reactions couldn't balance.

explanation: In a closed container, no material can go in or out. Products stay present to react in the reverse direction, so the forward and reverse reactions can come to balance each other.

prompt: At equilibrium, how does the rate of the forward reaction compare with the rate of the reverse reaction?

choices.text: They are equal.
The forward rate is always larger.
choices.why: If the forward rate were larger, there would still be a net reaction toward products.

choices.text: The reverse rate is always larger.
choices.why: If the reverse rate were larger, products would be turning back into reactants overall.

choices.text: Both are zero.
choices.why: Both reactions are still occurring at equilibrium.

explanation: At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so any overall change by one is canceled by the other.

prompt: The equilibrium SO2 + O2 ⇌ SO3 is balanced with the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of SO3?
explanation: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 has 2 S and 6 O on each side. An equilibrium equation must still be balanced.
